coredata.dc:description: Herein, a series of quaternized halloysite nanotubes (QHNTs) bearing different imidazoliums groups are prepared via distillation–precipitation polymerization and quaternarization, and then embedded into chitosan (CS) matrix to fabricate hybrid membranes. Systematic characterizations and measurements are performed to explore the relationships between the ligand of ammonium and the performance of hybrid membrane. It is found that QHNTs are well-dispersed within CS matrix, and the chain mobility of CS is promoted driven by repulsive interactions from QHNTs, in turn affording the increments of water uptake and area swelling. Together with the promoted chain mobility, low-barrier conduction pathways are formed along the QHNTs surface and then confer a significant enhancement in hydroxyl conductivity to hybrid membranes. For QHNTs, hydrophilic ligand could adsorb more water molecules and short ligand is more favorable for contacting with hydroxyl, both of which are beneficial for high hydroxyl conductivity. Particularly, incorporating 7.5% QHNTs with ester-type QA ligand endows the hybrid membrane with an 89% increase in conductivity from 0.009 to 0.017Scm−1 at 90°C and 100% RH. Yet under anhydrous conditions, the positive charge dispersity of QA and stereo-hindrance effect of the ligand are the predominant factors for hydroxyl ion hopping.

head.ce:title: Tuning the performance of anion exchange membranes by embedding multifunctional nanotubes into a polymer matrix

ce:affiliation.ce:textfn: School of Chemical Engineering and Energy, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou 450001, PR China

sa:affiliation.sa:organization: School of Chemical Engineering and Energy, Zhengzhou University

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Herein, a series of quaternized halloysite nanotubes (QHNTs) bearing different imidazoliums groups are prepared via distillation–precipitation polymerization and quaternarization, and then embedded into chitosan (CS) matrix to fabricate hybrid membranes. Systematic characterizations and measurements are performed to explore the relationships between the ligand of ammonium and the performance of hybrid membrane. It is found that QHNTs are well-dispersed within CS matrix, and the chain mobility of CS is promoted driven by repulsive interactions from QHNTs, in turn affording the increments of water uptake and area swelling. Together with the promoted chain mobility, low-barrier conduction pathways are formed along the QHNTs surface and then confer a significant enhancement in hydroxyl conductivity to hybrid membranes. For QHNTs, hydrophilic ligand could adsorb more water molecules and short ligand is more favorable for contacting with hydroxyl, both of which are beneficial for high hydroxyl conductivity. Particularly, incorporating 7.5% QHNTs with ester-type QA ligand endows the hybrid membrane with an 89% increase in conductivity from 0.009 to 0.017Scm−1 at 90°C and 100% RH. Yet under anhydrous conditions, the positive charge dispersity of QA and stereo-hindrance effect of the ligand are the predominant factors for hydroxyl ion hopping.

ce:section.ce:para: A fuel cell is an efficient energy conversion device which generates electric energy from chemical fuels and is considered to be promising for clean energy technology [1–3]. Among various fuel cells, proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) is most developed for the attractive system efficiencies and environmental benefits. However, due to the use of noble metals as catalyst and expensive polyelectrolyte membrane (e.g., Nafion), the high cost prohibits its widespread commercial adoption [4,5]. By comparison, alkaline fuel cell (AFC) has renewed growing attention on account of its faster kinetic rate for oxygen reduction and lower methanol crossover [6–8]. These features endow AFC with the following advantages: (i) higher cell voltages; (ii) more alternative catalysts (especially the cheaper non-noble metal catalysts); and (iii) lower usage amount of catalysts [9–13]. As the key component in AFC, anion exchange membrane (AEM) should possess high hydroxyl conductivity, excellent mechanical stability, and outstanding thermal stability. Particularly, adequate hydroxyl conductivity is highly required for AEM, as it determines the performance of AFC including the operational fuel cell voltage and current output.

During the past decades, tremendous efforts have been devoted to enhancing the hydroxyl conductivity of AEM. Polymers tethering organic cations have been demonstrated as solid AEMs for AFCs. These organic cations have been obtained by introducing quaternary ammonium (QA) [14,15], guandinium [16], or phosphonium groups [17] through chloromethylation of aromatic rings or bromination on the benzylic methyl groups of the polymers, followed by the menshutkin reaction. Various polymers, such as poly (olefin)s [18], poly (styrene)s [19], poly (phenylene oxide)s [20,21], poly (phenylene)s [22], and poly (aryleneether)s [23] have been investigated, which display a wide range of hydroxyl conductivities. A high hydroxyl conductivity can be acquired under high loading amount of organic cations, however, it generally leads to excessive water swelling and hence a loss of mechanical strength [12,24]. By comparison, organic–inorganic hybrid membranes have attracted intensive interest due to their promising advantages in enhancing physicochemical properties and providing ionic conductivity [25–27]. The as-utilized inorganic materials include TiO2 [28,29], SiO2 [30], nanotubes [31–33], hydroxyapatite (HAP) [34], montmorillonite [35], etc. Yang et al. embedded the hydrophilic HAP into crystalline PVA, in which HAP interfered with the segment configuration of PVA and decreased the crystallinity of the membrane, thus reducing the transfer energy barrier and enhancing the ionic conductivity [36]. In addition, they fabricated quaternary PVA–Al2O3 hybrid membrane with enhanced hydroxyl conductivity through similar method [37]. However, the incorporation of inorganic fillers (e.g., SiO2) into amorphous polymer matrix (e.g., quaternized chitosan) leads to the blockage for hydroxyl, resulting in the decrease of hydroxyl conductivity [38]. To address this issue, the filler materials bearing ion exchange groups have been adopted, which could provide additional ion hopping sites and conduction paths. For instance, Wang et al. prepared PVA/3- (trimethylammonium) propyl-functionalized silica hybrid membranes and found that 10% TMAPS could generate 70% increase of ionic conductivity [39]. Li and co-authors fabricated ionic liquid grafted carbon nanotubes (ILNTs) through radical polymerization, and noted that 0.3% ILNTs could elevate the conductivity of poly (2, 6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) containing imidazolium membrane from 0.0129 to 0.0252Scm−1 [40]. Despite of the advantages of functionalized filler-filled hybrid AEMs, the relevant investigation is seldom performed. In addition, the development of facile and general approach to fabricate efficient transfer channel remains a challenge at present.

Although the incorporation of functionalized inorganic fillers into polymer matrix may create ion transfer channels at the polymer/filler interface, the rational design of filler functionality based on hydroxyl ion transfer mechanism remains challenging. Actually, the filler functionality affects both the chemical environment and water environment of ion transfer channel, which are further in close relationship with ionic transfer mechanism. Generally, the transfer of hydroxyl ions through AEM obeys the following mechanisms [41]: Grotthuss mechanism, surface site hopping, diffusion and migration, and convection. Among them, the former two are regarded as predominant mechanisms. Grotthuss mechanism is assumed that the hydroxyl diffuses through the hydrogen-bonded networks formed by water. The transfer process follows the hydrogen bond rearrangement, re-orientation, and hydroxyl ion transfer by forming a tetrahedrally coordinated water cluster. Surface site hopping is related to the hydroxyl ion hopping from one cationic group to a neighboring one. This would to be the dominating transfer mechanism when the membrane is operated under anhydrous conditions. It reveals that water plays an indispensable role in the transfer of hydroxide. According to the aforementioned mechanisms, QA as the most employed hydroxyl ion carrier needs delicate design for intensifying Grotthuss mechanism and surface hopping mechanism. By varying the steric conformation and the polarity of the ligand on N atom of QA, its capacity of binding water molecule or hydroxyl ion can be tailored, and therefore the optimal ion transfer channel structures are expected to be acquired. However, the effect of ligand type of QA on the hydroxyl ion transfer channel environment has neither been theoretically predicted nor experimentally demonstrated.

In this study, novel polymer-nanotube hybrid AEM was prepared by embedding quaternized nanotubes into polymer matrix, in which the nanotubes might create continuous transfer pathways due to their high aspect ratios. Halloysite nanotubes (HNTs), naturally two-layered aluminosilicate clay mineral and available in abundance in the world, were chosen due to their excellent mechanical/thermal stabilities and sufficient Si–OH and Al–OH groups [42,43]. Imidazoliums were chosen as functional groups due to the good alkaline stability and high quaternarization reactivity from imidazole [44,45]. HNTs were quaternized via a facile distillation–precipitation polymerization followed by Menshutkin reaction using four chlorinated reagents. In such a way, four kinds of polymeric layer bearing high QA loading amount but different chemical structures were grafted on HNTs surface. Chitosan (CS) was chosen as membrane matrix due to its good film forming and mechanical properties as well as low cost [46,47]. To better investigate the function and transfer mechanism of QA, CS was not quaternized to minimize its influence on ionic conduction of the hybrid membrane. The microstructures and physicochemical properties of the membranes were investigated in detail. Additionally, the hydroxyl conductivities and transfer mechanism of the membranes at different temperatures and humidity were systematically evaluated.

Halloysite nanotubes were refined from clay minerals in Henan province, China. CS with the deacetylation degree of 91% was purchased from Golden-Shell Biochemical Co. (Zhejiang, China) and used as received. 3-(Methacryloxy) propyltrimethoxysilane (MPS) was purchased from Aldrich and distilled under vacuum. 2, 2-Azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN), ethylene glycol dimethyl acrylate (EGDMA) and acetonitrile were obtained from Kewei Chemistry Co. Ltd (Tianjin, China). Vinyl imidazole (VI), chlorobutane (CB), chlorodecane (CD), benzyl chloride (BC) and ethyl chloroformate (EC) were purchased from xi ya reagent in Shandong province, China. De-ionized water was used throughout the experiment.

ce:section.ce:section-title: 2.2. Synthesis of the quaternized halloysite nanotubes (QHNTs)
ce:section.ce:para: QHNTs were synthesized via distillation-precipitation polymerization and quaternarization method. The detailed test method are as follows: HNTs (3.0g) were dispersed into ethanol (160mL), then water (15mL) and aqueous solution of ammonium (12mL) were added into the solution and stirring at room temperature (20–25°C) for 24h. Then, MPS (1.0mL) was added into the mixture and being stirred for another 32h. Subsequently, the MPS modified HNTs (M-HNTs) were purified by three cycles of centrifugation and followed by drying in vacuum oven at 40°C. M-HNTs (0.30g), EGDMA (0.30mL), VI (0.60mL), and AIBN (0.016g) were dispersed into acetonitrile (80mL) in a dried stand-up round bottom flask. The above mixture was heated and kept at 82°C until half acetonitrile was distilled out. Afterwards, the N-vinyl imidazole grafted HNTs (VI-HNTs) was purified by centrifugation with washing by acetonitrile, and then dried in vacuum drying oven. VI-HNTs (0.6g) was dispersed into absolute alcohol (100mL), then quantitative of quaternary aminating reagent (CB, CD, EC, BC) (QA/VI=1:1, mol/mol) was added into the solution and the solution was refluxed under 80°C for 8h, QHNTs were purified by centrifugation with washing by ethanol and dried in vacuum oven. It should be noted that the preparation conditions of QHNTs were selected and controlled for achieving similar amount of QA for all the QHNTs. The as-synthesized QHNTs were designated as C4-QHNTs, C10-QHNTs, E-QHNTs, and B-QHNTs, respectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: 2.3. Preparation of CS control and hybrid membranes
ce:section.ce:para: CS (1.2g) was dissolved into acetic acid aqueous solution (2%, 50mL) under stirring at 80°C for 2h. Simultaneously, a certain amount of HNTs or QHNTs were dispersed into deionized water (10mL) with ultrasonic treatment for 6h, then added into CS solution drop-wise. The mixture was stirred vigorously at 80°C for another 2h. Subsequently, cooled down to room temperature (20–25°C), a given amount of cross-linker glutaraldehyde (GA, 2%, v/v) aqueous solution was added to the mixture and stirred vigorously at room temperature (20–25°C) for 3h, and then ultrasonic treatment for another 30min. The resultant mixture was cast onto a glass plate until the solvent evaporate at room temperature completely. For CS control membrane, the casting solution was prepared without the addition of nanofillers and the preparation process was as mentioned above. All the membranes were immersed into 0.5molL−1 KOH solution at room temperature for 24h to obtain hydroxyl form membranes, and then washed thoroughly with de-ionized water to remove the residual KOH in the membrane. Finally, the membrane was dried at 40°C until a constant weight was reached. The average thickness of the dry membranes fell in the range of 60–65μm. The nanohybrid membranes obtained were designated as CS/HNTs-X, CS/C4-QHNTs-X, CS/C10-QHNTs-X, CS/E-QHNTs-X and CS/B-QHNTs-X, where X (X=2.5, 5, 7.5 and 10) represented the weight percentage of nanofillers to CS.

ce:section.ce:section-title: 2.4. Characterization of the nanotubes and membranes
ce:section.ce:para: The size and morphology of HNTs and QHNTs were observed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G220 S-TWIN). The chemical compositions of nanotubes and membranes were determined by a Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR, NicoletMAGNA-IR560) with the range of 4000–400cm−1 at room temperature. The surface and cross-section images of membranes were obtained on a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Nanosem430). The sample was freeze-fractured in liquid nitrogen and then sputtered with gold prior to measurement. Thermo gravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) were carried out to analyze the thermal stability of CS control and hybrid membranes. TGA was conducted using a TGA-50SHIMADZU, operating from 25 to 800°C at a heating rate of 10°Cmin−1 under nitrogen atmosphere. DSC was obtained on a 204F1NETZSCH and the sample first preheated from room temperature to 130°C at a heating rate of 10°Cmin−1 under nitrogen atmosphere, then cooled to 90°C and reheated to 260°C. Mechanical property of the membrane (1.0cm×4.0cm) was tested by Instron mechanical tester (Testometric 350 AX) with the elongation rate of 5.0mmmin−1 under room temperature.

Water uptake of the membrane was carried out by sorption method. The membrane samples were soaked in de-ionized water for 24h at room temperature to monitor the weight of the wet membranes and were measured rapidly after wiping the excessive surface water with a tissue paper. The hydroxyl conductivities of the membranes were measured by using alternating current (AC). The impedance was determined with a frequency response analyzer (FRA, compactstat, IVIUMTech.). The impedance was measured within a frequency range of 100KHz to 100Hz with perturbation voltage amplitude of 20mV. Resistance value associated with the membrane conductivity was obtained from the intercept of impedance at high frequency. The relative humidity (RH) was kept at about 100% by using water vapor and the testing temperature was controlled from 25 to 90°C. The hydroxyl conductivity of the membrane was calculated by Eq. (4):

Four kinds of QHNTs are prepared as illustrated in Scheme1a: the first step is the grafting of MPS onto the surface of HNTs to introduce reactive vinyl groups; the second step is the formation of polymer electrolyte layer through distillation–precipitation polymerization with the aid of vinyl groups to capture the newly formed oligomers and monomers; and the third step is the synthesis of QHNTs through Menshutkin reaction using CB, CD, EC, and BC as quaternary aminating reagents.

The morphologies of HNTs and QHNTs are observed by TEM images, as shown in Fig. 1. It can be found that HNTs (Fig. 1a) possess well-defined tubular structure with 800nm in length and 60nm in diameter. After surface modification, a clear polymeric layer with the average thickness of 10nm is observed on the surface of QHNTs (Fig. 1b). Meanwhile, QHNTs still keep their tubular structure without obvious destruction after polymerization, as the polymerization mainly occurs on the vinyl groups of MPS on HNTs surface.

Chemical structure and weight content of the polyelectrolyte layer on QHNTs were determined by FTIR and TGA analyses, respectively. Fig. 2a shows that the FTIR spectrum of HNTs shows two characteristic bands at 1035 and 912cm−1, corresponding to the bending of Si–O–Si stretching and Al–O deformation, respectively [50]. By comparison, QHNTs show characteristic bands at 1568 and 745cm−1 due to the imidazolium cation, while the band at 745cm−1 is overlapped by the strong and broad band of HNTs [44,51,52]. Besides, the characteristic band for absorbed water near 3453cm−1 become stronger after QA modification due to the presence of hydrophilic imidazolium cations. A new band appears at 3046–2890cm−1 in the spectra of QHNTs, which is assigned to the typical stretching vibration of C–H. By comparison, the band intensity of C4-QHNTs and C10-QHNTs become stronger due to the higher content of C–H. E-QHNTs give rise to two characteristic bands of ester carbonyl group at 1731 and 1220cm−1. B-QHNTs give rise to several weak characteristic bands in the range of 1590–1410cm−1, which are assigned to the typical vibration of phenyl groups.

TGA curves in Fig. 2b reveal that HNTs display two-stage weight loss, while QHNTs display three-stage weight loss. For HNTs, the first stage (30–200°C) is assigned to the evaporation of adsorbed water within the nanotubes, and the second stage (385–800°C) corresponds to decomposition of organic components in nanotubes. Similarly to that of HNTs, for QHNTs, the first-stage (30–200°C) is mainly attributed to the evaporation of adsorbed water within the nanotubes. The weight loss for QHNTs (5%) is higher than that of HNTs (3%) due to the high water absorbing capability of quaternary ammonium imidazole groups. The second stage (200–385°C) is mainly assigned to the decomposition of polymer layer on the surface of QHNTs. The third stage (385–800°C) is due to the decomposition of organic components in nanotubes. Compared to HNTs, the decomposition of polymer components affords QHNTs lower char yields at 800°C. According to the char yields, the weight percentage of polymer layer in C4-QHNTs, C10-HNTs, E-QHNTs and B-QHNTs are calculated to be approximately 37.9%, 37.0%, 38.6%, and 39.4%, respectively. The close weight percentage suggests the similar structure for all the QHNTs, helped by the same preparation procedure.

The synthesis mechanism of the membranes is shown in Scheme 1b. The HNTs and QHNTs were embedded into CS matrix to prepare hybrid membranes via solution casting method. The cross-sectional microstructures of hybrid membranes are shown in Fig. 3. Fig. 3a shows that CS control membrane is dense and smooth, without obvious cracks or pinholes. By comparison, the cross-sections of hybrid membranes become rougher and display obvious wrinkles due to the presence of nanotubes. As can be seen in Fig. 3b, HNTs display poor dispersion within CS matrix. Such phenomenon is ascribed to their weak interfacial compatibility, which increases the surface tension of HNTs and thus results in the formation of nanotube agglomerations. By comparison, QHNTs can disperse uniformly in polymer matrix, since the presence of organic polymer layer can reduce the surface Gibbs energy and improve the interfacial compatibility. Noting that increasing the content of nanotubes would cause serious agglomerations within hybrid membrane, so the filler content is kept below 10% in this study. In addition, QHNTs maintain their intact tubular structure without destruction, ensuring their ability to create continuous ion conductive channels within CS bulk.

The interfacial interaction between nanotubes and CS is probed by FTIR and the results are shown in Fig. 4. The characteristic bands for CS at 3457, 1643, and 1579cm−1 are observed for all the membranes, corresponding to the hydroxyl, amide I, and amide II groups, respectively [53]. Compared with CS control membrane, an elevated intensity of the characteristic band at 1579cm−1(–NH2) can be observed in the spectra of all the CS/QHNTs. This phenomenon may be understood as that: during the membrane preparation, the amino groups in CS would be partially protonated to –NH3 + in acid solution [54]. After the incorporation of QHNTs, the subsequent introduction of QAICs would generate electrostatic repulsive force to CS chains, which inhibits the formation of hydrogen bonds (–OH/–NH2) among CS chains. This could also be verified by the decreased crystalline of hybrid membranes as proved by XRD results. Consequently, the amount of free amino groups in CS/QHNTs would increase, and the band intensity for amino group at 1579cm−1 is a little stronger than that of CS control membrane. Further evidence for the interfacial interactions in hybrid membranes can be obtained by DSC results. Similar observations have been reported in other CS-based hybrid membranes [55]. In contrast, the bond intensities of –OH and –NH2 groups all become weaker with the addition of HNTs. This is reasonably originated from the formation of hydrogen bonds between the –OH on HNTs and the –OH/–NH2 on CS chains, thus reducing the amount of free –OH and –NH2 groups. In addition, the characteristic band for adsorbed water near 3457cm−1 also becomes slightly stronger when embedding QHNTs. The influence of nanotube content on FTIR spectra was performed using CS/E-QHNTs as representatives, and the results are shown in Fig. 4b. The band intensity at 1643 and 1579cm−1 is only slightly altered with the filler content increasing. No new band appears in the spectra of hybrid membrane, indicating that the HNTs and QHNTs are physically mixed with CS matrix without forming chemical bonds.

ce:section.ce:section-title: 3.3. Thermal and mechanical properties of the membranes
ce:section.ce:para: As the key element of fuel cell, AEMs must have excellent thermal and mechanical stabilities for long-time operation. Thermal properties of the as-prepared membranes are investigated by TGA and DSC analyses, and the results are shown in Fig. 5(a)–(d), respectively. All the membranes undergo three-stage weight loss. The first stage is water evaporation from membrane around 30–200°C. During this stage, HNTs-filled membranes show lower weight loss (about 5%) compared with CS control membrane (about 7%), whereas QHNTs-filled membranes exhibit higher weight loss (9–11%). The hydrophilic polymer layer and promoted chain mobility co-contribute to the high water adsorption capability of QHNTs-filled membranes. This is in agreement with the TGA results of the QHNTs (Fig. 2b). The second stage is the degradation of side-chains of CS and polymer layer of QHNTs around 230–340°C. As shown in Fig. 5a, the degradation temperature of CS/QHNTs is lower than that of CS control membrane. This phenomenon is probably ascribed to the promotion of the chain mobility at CS–QHNTs interfacial region, which could be confirmed by DSC results. In addition, XRD results suggest that the crystalline of the hybrid membrane decreases due to the steric interference of QHNTs, thus resulting in a slight reduction of the thermal stability of CS/QHNTs. Similar observations have been reported in other hybrid membranes [56–58]. By comparison, HNTs display opposite function in altering the chain packing via hydrogen-bond interaction, and the chain mobility would be restrained. As a result, CS/HNTs gives a little higher degradation temperature. The third stage is the degradation of polymer backbone of CS around 480–800°C. The stable inorganic nanotubes donate a little higher char yields on the hybrid membranes. The influence of filler content on thermal degradation behavior is shown in Fig. 5b. It can be found that the thermal degradation mechanism of hybrid membranes is almost unchanged with the nanotube content increase. Higher nanotube content gives higher char yield at 800°C to hybrid membranes. Although the thermostability of hybrid membrane slightly decreases with the addition of QHNTs, the CS/QHNTs are thermally stable up to 230°C, adequate for the application of AFC (60–90°C).

The chain mobility of CS in membrane is directly probed by DSC (Fig. 5(c) and (d)). A clear transition temperature at 170.7°C is observed in the DSC curve of CS control membrane, which is assigned to the dissociation process of inter-chain hydrogen bonding of chitosan [59,60]. The incorporation of HNTs elevates this temperature to about 176.5°C, confirming the inhibition of chain mobility of CS [61]. By comparison, the presence of QHNTs promotes the chain mobility, affording a reduction of the transition temperature to below 170.7°C. As the interfacial repulsions increases with QHNTs content increase, the transition temperatures of CS/QHNTs reduce gradually. For instance, the transition temperatures of CS/E-QHNTs decrease from 164.6 to 156.1°C when increasing the E-QHNTs content from 2.5% to 10% (Fig. 5(d)). For the four kinds of CS/QHNTs, their transition temperatures decrease in the order of CS/C4-QHNTs<CS/B-QHNTs<CS/E-QHNTs<CS/C10-QHNTs. Generally, ester group and benzyl are electron-withdrawing groups, while n-butyl and decyl are electron-donating groups. Accordingly, ethyl formate and benzyl can decrease the electron density of N atom in QAICs and improve their electro positivity, thus generating stronger repulsions with CS chains. In comparison, the polar of benzyl is weaker than ester group. Therefore, the chain mobility in CS/B-QHNTs is weaker than that in CS/E-QHNTs. For alkane type QAICs, long side chains will produce shielding effect and increase the steric hindrance, resulting in decreased electrostatic repulsions with CS chains. The most perverse is that the transition temperature of CS/C10-QHNT is lower than those of other hybrid membranes, probably due to that the long alkyl chains insert into CS matrix, and then interfere with its chain configuration.

Fig. 5(e) and (f) shows the stress–strain curves of the as-prepared membranes for probing their mechanical properties. CS control membrane exhibits acceptable mechanical stability with Young's modulus of 787.8MPa, along with the tensile strength of 43.1MPa and the elongation at break of 13.6%. The tensile strength of CS control membrane is much higher than that of Nafion117 (15.03MPa) [38]. By comparison, the hybrid membranes acquire slightly enhanced mechanical stabilities. For instance, incorporating 5% HNTs, C4-QHNTs, C10-QHNTs, E-QHNTs and B-QHNTs elevate the tensile strength to 51.7, 45.1, 48.9, 43.6 and 44.9MPa, along with Young's modulus of 1100, 817.3, 806.5, 820.7 and 824.5MPa, respectively. The variation of mechanical properties of CS/QHNTs due to the difference of interfacial interaction between CS and QHNTs. Fig. 5(f) shows that Young's modulus of hybrid membranes (CS/E-QHNTs) decreases with the increase of filler content. For instance, the Young's modulus of CS/E-QHNTs decreases from 1020 to 840MPa when the filler content increases from 2.5% to 10%. By comparison, the tensile strength of the hybrid membrane increases due to the enhancement of the steric interference.

For directly probing the CS chain packing, the crystalline properties are inspected through the XRD technique. For an AEM, high crystallinity generally exhibits low ionic migration rate and is not suitable for fuel cell. Fig. 6 shows that all the membranes exhibit characteristic bands of CS phase at 2θ=15.3°, 20.1°, and 20.6°, which is mainly maintained by the intermolecular hydrogen bonds [61]. The characteristic bands of CS matrix become weaker when adding HNTs and QHNTs, which interferes with the ordered packing of CS chains through the interfacial interactions and steric effects. With the increase of filler content, the interference effect enhances and the crystallinity in hybrid membrane gradually reduces (Fig. 6(b)). Similar observation has been reported in other CS-based hybrid membranes [62].

ce:section.ce:section-title: 3.5 Water uptake, swelling and IEC of the membranes
ce:section.ce:para: Since water molecules participate in the ionic transfer via the Grotthuss, Diffusion, and Migration types, water uptake is a crucial parameter for AEMs. Fig. 7a reveals that CS control membrane attains a water uptake of 79.2% at 25°C by the hydrophilic groups (i.e., –OH, –NH2 and –NH3 +). CS/HNTs display lower water uptake, resulting from the suppressed chain motion of CS and the consequent water absorption ability. Upon surface modification, the incorporation of QHNTs endows CS/QHNTs with higher water uptakes probably due to the hydrophilic polymer layer and promoted CS chain motion. Such phenomenon is in accordance with the results of TGA analysis. As for the four kinds of functional groups, the polar of the ligand on QAICs increase in the order of C4=C10<B<E, and the water uptakes of CS/QHNTs hybrid membranes follow the order of CS/C4-QHNTs<CS/C10-QHNTs<CS/B-QHNTs<CS/E-QHNTs. This is probably because that with the increase of polarity of the side chain, the hydrophilic ability of the imidazole cations is strengthened. The water uptakes of CS/QHNTs will further increase when increasing the filler content. For instance, elevating the E-QHNTs content from 2.5% to 10% increases the water uptakes from 87.5% to 98.1%.

Generally, the adsorption of water would cause the membrane to swell through hydration, and higher water uptake usually affords higher area swelling. Similar to the water uptake behavior, Fig. 7(b) shows that the swelling ratios increase in the order of CS/C4-QHNTs<CS/C10-QHNTs<CS/B-QHNTs<CS/E-QHNTs. Comparing the water adsorption and chain swelling of CS/C4-QHNTs and CS/C10-QHNTs, it can be found that growing the hydrophobic chain segments in QHNTs would enhance the chain mobility of CS.

IEC that reflects the number of ion exchangeable groups and the available hydroxyl ions determines the anion transfer ability, especially for surface site hopping mechanism. IEC values of these membranes are measured by classical titration method, as shown in Fig. 7c. CS control membrane displays an IEC of 0.36mmolg−1, close to the value in literature [66]. By comparison, the IEC values of CS/QHNTs are elevated on account of the introduction of numerous QAICs and the reduction of CS crystallinity. Meanwhile, the IEC values could be facilely tuned by the QHNTs content. For instance, the IEC values are 0.37, 0.378, 0.387, and 0.4mmolg−1 when incorporates 2.5%, 5%, 7.5%, and 10% E-QHNTs, respectively. Compared with the IEC values in literatures ( Table 1), the IEC values of the as-prepared membranes are comparable to those of other membranes. For CS/QHNTs, their IEC values vary with the QAICs type and follow the order of CS/C4-QHNTs>CS/C10-QHNTs>CS/B-QHNTs>CS/E-QHNTs. For alkyl substituent group, positive charge is concentrated on the N atoms, which has strong affinity ability for hydroxyl ions. However, excessive carbon chain will decrease the ion exchange capability as the obvious steric hindrance is generated. For CS/B-QHNTs, the positive charge is dispersed by the delocalization effect of benzene ring, which weakens their affinity ability to OH−. E-QHNTs-filled membrane displays the lowest ion exchange capacity, since ester groups are partially hydrolyzed into carboxyl and subsequent amphoteric ion. The non-conductive feature of HNTs makes the IEC values of CS/HNTs (below 0.35mmolg−1) lower than that of CS control membrane. And the value continuously reduces from 0.35 to 0.32mmolg−1 as HNTs content increases from 2.5% to 10%.

As the performance-limiting parameters for AEMs, hydroxyl conductivities of the as-prepared membranes at 25°C and 100% RH are shown in Fig. 8a. Theoretically, Grotthuss mechanism and surface site hopping are the dominant mechanisms for hydroxyl transfer through AEM. The results reveal that CS control membrane attains a hydroxyl conductivity of 0.002Scm−1, which is close to the value in literature [63]. Compared with CS control membrane, CS/QHNTs acquire higher hydroxyl conduction properties. For instance, 2.5% C4-QHNTs, C10-QHNTs, E-QHNTs, and B-QHNTs elevates the conductivities of hybrid membranes to 0.00398, 0.00356, 0.00452, and 0.003Scm−1, respectively. Compared with the data of other hybrid membranes in literatures, it seems that CS/QHNTs possess comparable ionic conductivities [72–74]. Such phenomenon should be attributed to the enhanced water uptake and polymer chain mobility of the hybrid membranes upon QHNTs incorporation, and as a result, more transfer sites have been introduced into the membranes. What's more, QHNTs with high aspect ratios, which allow the formation of long-range uninterrupted pathways with the aid of absorbed water and QAICs, significantly promotes the transmission rate of hydroxyl ions in the membrane. It can be observed that the hydroxyl conductivities of the hybrid membranes increase by increasing the amount of QHNTs when the content is lower than 7.5wt%. Such phenomenon indicates that the conductivities can be enhanced by increasing the IEC values of the membranes. However, the conductivities of the hybrid membranes decrease when the content of QHNTs is higher than 7.5%. The decrease of conductivity may relate to the agglomeration of the QHNTs in the CS matrix, leading to the blocking effect on the ion transport. For instance, the hydroxyl ion conductivity of CS/E-QHNTs decreases from 5.56×10− 3 Scm−1 to 5.15×10− 3 Scm-1 when the filler content increases from 7.5% to 10%. Different from QHNTs, the incorporation of HNTs decline the hydroxyl conductivity of CS/HNTs, attributing to the low IEC and restrained CS chain mobility.

Ion transfer site plays a critical role in hydroxyl conduction when the OH− transfer via surface hopping mechanisms, while the chemical structure of the ligand affects the conduction ability of QAICs. For CS/QHNTs, the diverse in hydroxyl conductivities on account of the different chemical and water environments in the membrane follows the order of CS/B-QHNTs<CS/C10-QHNTs<CS/C4-QHNTs<CS/E-QHNTs. The full swelling of the membrane intimately affects the mediation of water on the transmission of OH-. The hydroxyl conductivity of CS/C4-QHNTs is higher than CS/C10-QHNTs under the same content. This finding is probably due to that n-butyl and decyl are nonpolar groups having the same induction effect on imidazole group but possessing different length of carbon chain. Prolonging the carbon chain would strengthen the space screening effects for QA groups capturing hydroxyl ions. Comparing CS/E-QHNTs and CS/B-QHNTs, ester group has strong polarity effect than benzyl and meanwhile it may partially hydrolysis under alkaline condition. The formation of amphoteric ion is in favor of the mediation of water, promoting the transfer of hydroxyl ions. While benzyl, having strong steric hindrance and polarity entrainment, will increase the electropositivity of B-QHNTs, which is against the hydroxyl conduction. In a nutshell, the quaternary ammonium cation with the hydrophilic side chain is in favor of the hydroxyl conduction.

To further investigate hydroxyl ion conduction ability of QA groups, the hydroxyl conductivity of these membranes are tested at 25°C under anhydrous condition, as shown in Fig. 8b. It is found that CS control membrane exhibits a conductivity of 1.94×10−7 Scm−1, much lower than that under 100% RH. This finding indicates that water plays an important role on the hydroxyl conduction. CS/HNTs display lower hydroxyl conduction properties than CS control membrane due to the presence of non-conductive HNTs. In comparison, CS/QHNTs exhibit higher hydroxyl conductivities on account of the continuous transfer channels using the QA groups. The hydroxyl conductivities of these membranes follow the order of CS/B-QHNTs <CS/C10-QHNTs<CS/E-QHNTs<CS/C4-QHNTs. The hydroxyl transfer through the membrane mainly occurs on surface hopping method under anhydrous condition. The chemical structure of QA group on QHNTs plays a determinant role in hydroxyl transfer. For B-QHNTs, the electron cloud density of N atom in QA is decreasing due to the delocalization effect of benzene ring, which is infaust for the hydroxyl conduction. With the length of alkane increasing, the obvious steric screening effect is unfavorable for the OH- transfer. As for E-QHNTs, due to the formation of zwitterion, the hydroxyl ion hopping among the groups is expected to be impeded on account of the electronegative carboxylate group.

The temperature-dependent conductivities under hydrated condition are also measured, as shown in Fig. 8(c) and (d). It is found that all the membranes exhibit gradual increase of conductivity with the temperatures varying from 25 to 90°C, resulting from the promoted motion of polymer chains and water molecules at high temperature. For instance, the conductivity of CS control membrane increases from 0.002 to 0.009Scm−1. By comparison, CS/QHNTs possesses higher conductivity than that of CS control membrane under every testing temperature, and the maximum conductivity is obtain by CS/E-QHNTs-7.5% of 0.017Scm−1 under 90°C and 100% RH.

For further investigating the energy needed for hydroxyl transfer, the hydroxyl conductivities in Arrhenius plot are shown in Fig. 9, from which the values of activation energy (E
a , Table 2) are calculated using Arrhenius equation. CS control membrane has the E
a of 22.3kJmol−1. By comparison, the E
a values of CS/HNTs increase to the range of 23.8–26.6kJmol−1. While for CS/QHNTs, the E
a values decrease to the range of 19.3–15.2kJmol−1, which is close to the E
a values reported in other literatures [19,77]. The reduced E
a implies that the QHNTs create efficient conduction pathways for ion transfer along the nanotube surface. Increasing the QHNTs content gives more pathways to hybrid membrane, resulting in a gradual reduction of E
a value. For instance, the E
a values of CS/E-QHNTs decrease from 16.4 to 15.2kJmol−1 when increasing the filler content from 2.5% to 7.5%. Comparing the four kinds of hybrid membranes, CS/E-QHNTs displays the lowest E
a values due to the appropriate chemical environment and water environment in the membrane. For alkyl side chain, the transfer resistance increases with the increase of the length of side chain and therefore generate higher E
a value. Among the four QHNTs, the B-QHNTs makes CS/B-QHNTs possess the highest E
a values, probably due to the incongruous space structure of the transfer sites for the hydroxyl conduction.

Sufficient stability of hydroxyl conductivity of AAEM is curial to stable performances of a fuel cell. Fig. 10 shows the time-dependent hydroxyl conductivities of CS control and hybrid membranes after treatment with 1M KOH at 80°C for several days. It can be found that no obvious decrease of the conductivity is observed for the as-prepared control and hybrid membranes, indicating a good chemical stability of the membrane in KOH solution. The good alkaline stability of the hybrid membrane is due to the resonance effect of the conjugated imidazole rings, which reduces the positive charge density of the cation and weakens the interaction with OH− [82,83]. In addition, imidazoliums are grafted onto the surface of HNTs through covalent bond, by which the leakages of imidazoliums are effectively avoided.

In this study, quaternized HNTs with four different kinds of imidazolium cations have been synthesized and then embedded into CS matrix to prepare novel hybrid AAEMs. By altering the property of ligand of imidazolium cations, the quaternized nanotubes are found to construct efficient ion transfer channels with well-defined chemical environment and water environment: (1) polar ligand on the N atom can enrich water molecules around the imidazolium group under hydrous condition, in favor of the mediation of water and OH− conductivity; (2) small ligand can reduce the steric hindrance against OH− approach, and thus facilitate OH− hopping; (3) ligand with negative electricity or electron withdrawing effect go against the OH− conduction, indicating the pivotal role of electrical property and spatial structure of the transfer sites in OH− conduction. In this sense, among the four types of ligands (namely butyl, decyl, carbethoxyl, and benzyl groups), we find that carbethoxyl group is the optimal ligand for OH− conduction under hydrated conditions. In addition, the hybrid membrane exhibits good operational stability under harsh alkaline conditions. Constructing continuous transfer pathways along with appropriate water and chemical environments in the membrane may offer a promising approach for designing high-performance AEMs.
